newsitem.title: USA: FDA proposes to withdraw Seldane approval.
newsitem.headline: FDA proposes to withdraw Seldane approval.

text.p: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration Monday took a step toward taking a leading allergy medicine, Seldane, off the market because it can interact with other drugs and cause a potentially fatal heart condition.
The FDA said it intends to withdraw its approval of Seldane and Seldane D antihistimine and generic versions, all of which contain terfenadine.

Revoking marketing approval can take several months but the FDA said patients using Seldane or its equivalent should talk to their doctors about alternative treatments, including the drug Allegra, which came on the U.S. market last summer.
Millions of people have taken Seldane, the first medicine to control hay fever and similar allergies without causing drowsiness. At one point, it was among the top 10 drugs in the United States.

But after Seldane went on the market in 1985, the FDA began getting reports of life-threatening heartbeat irregularities when it is taken with other common drugs, including the antibiotic erythromicin and the antifungal ketoconozole. It can also be hazardous for people with liver disease.

The FDA has received several hundred reports of cardiac and other problems in patients taking Seldane, including fatalities. But FDA officials said it was not certain that all of those so-called "adverse incidents" were definitively caused by the antihistamine.
Hoechst Marion Roussel of Kansas City, which markets the drug, defended Seldane's safety when used properly.
The FDA said that educational campaigns, including labeling changes and statements warning of the drug interaction risks, have reduced but not eliminated the problem.
The Hoechst unit recently introduced Allegra as an alternative to Seldane. Allegra contains a different ingredient, fexofenadine, which does not cause the same dangerous interactions, the FDA said.
The company Monday announced a promotional campaign to switch patients from Seldane to Allegra, which has been available in U.S. drugstores since last August.
However, it defended Seldane's safety and said in a statement that it would "aggressively defend the product and continues to stand firmly behind the safety of Seldane.
"Seldane is safe and effective when used in accordance with the package insert," the company added.
Seldane's U.S. sales in 1995 were $400 million, down from a peak of $600 million earlier.
When the first reports of problems came in, the FDA responded with an education campaign, preferring not to take the drug off the market when the benefits outweighed the risks.
Once Allegra became available, however, that equation changed, FDA officials said.
The FDA notice gives the manufacturers of medicines containing terfenadine 30 days to request a hearing to show why approval should not be withdrawn.
